question.problem: Starting with the standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ find the first three non-zero terms of the series expansion for $\int \sqrt{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
The series expansion of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{5!}{x}^{5}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $\sqrt{x}$ in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{x} & =\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3!}(\sqrt{x})^{3}+\frac{1}{5!}(\sqrt{x})^{5}-⋯ \\  & ={x}^{1/2}-\frac{1}{3!}({x}^{1/2})^{3}+\frac{1}{5!}({x}^{1/2})^{5}-⋯ \\  & ={x}^{1/2}-\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{120}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply the series by $\sqrt{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{x} & =\sqrt{x}\cdot ({x}^{1/2}-\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{120}-⋯) \\  & ={x}^{1/2}\cdot ({x}^{1/2}-\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{120}-⋯) \\  & ={x}^{2/2}-\frac{{x}^{4/2}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{6/2}}{120}-⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{120}-⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, integrating with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{120}-⋯)\text{d}x \\  & =C+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6\cdot 3}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{120\cdot 4}-⋯ \\  & =C+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{18}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{480}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$
